description: Lumo is an AI companion app for astronauts on long-duration missions.
summary:
Mental health is often neglected on Earth, yet it is clear that it can be more lethal than routine ailments. Considering that crew members come from different backgrounds, are away from their families, and face new changes every second, addressing astronauts' mental well-being is essential. To support this, we have designed Lumo.
Lumo is an astronaut mental health monitor that spots early signs of stress, fatigue and social withdrawal during long-duration missions without asking crew to fill out forms. Instead of adding tasks, it uses signals that astronauts already produce from their speech, their sleep and disparity in their performance patterns of short cognitive checks. It is designed to run onboard, so it keeps working when communication with Earth is delayed or lost, as on a Mars mission. Each astronaut sees a Green, Yellow or Red status, a one-sentence reason and a specific action, such as a lighter workload or private family time. Ground teams receive a report only if the astronaut chooses to share it. Lumo builds on NASA research such as STRESSnet and WinSCAT, and aims to tell WinSCAT when to run instead of waiting for a fixed monthly test. Our working prototype demonstrates the astronaut using simulated data.
details:
What it does and how it works
Lumo combines three passive data channels:

  • Voice and text: language markers of anxiety, cognitive load, social withdrawal and attention drift, analysed locally. No raw audio leaves the device.
  • Sleep and physiology: sleep duration, efficiency and heart rate variability from wearables such as the Oura Ring, which the ISS National Lab has tested.
  • Cognitive micro-tests: a 3–5 minute abbreviated WinSCAT-style check, triggered only when voice and sleep signals look abnormal.

Lumo compares each astronaut's own baseline, not a population norm. When signals agree, such as slower speech plus reduced deep sleep, confidence in the status rises. The astronaut gets a status, a reason and an action.

What we built
A working prototype with two interfaces:

  • An astronaut view with a status card, passive insights, recommendations and an auto-adjust schedule.
  • A ground-control view where an operator feeds simulated crew data, watches baseline confidence build and sees suggested actions.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Catches problems earlier, between monthly cognitive tests.
  • Works with communication delays, because decisions happen on board.
  • Adds no workload and no questionnaires.
  • Respects privacy and autonomy, which should help crew trust and use it.
  • Helps explain why a test result is off (fatigue, stress or something else), which WinSCAT alone cannot do.

The longer-term aim is better crew wellbeing and mission safety on Moon and Mars missions, and possibly on Earth in isolated or high-stress workplaces.

Tools and technology

  • HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript, with browser, local, storage for the demo database.
  • A presentation deck
  • Planned, not built: local lightweight NLP with the STRESSnet lexicon, wearable integration, an abbreviated WinSCAT with dynamic triggering, a rule engine in phase 1 and personalized machine learning in phase 2.

What is creative about it

  • Dynamic cognitive testing: signals decide when to test, not the calendar.
  • Cross-checking voice, sleep and performance together.
  • Astronaut-first privacy, where the person decides what leaves the habitat.
  • A one-sentence explanation and a concrete action, not a dashboard of scores.

Factors we considered

  • Communication delay and limited bandwidth, so on-board processing and syncing only trend indicators.
  • Privacy, autonomy and trust within a small crew.
  • False positives and false negatives. Lumo is decision support for the crew, not a diagnostic tool.
  • Individual differences, accents and languages, which can bias language analysis.
  • Evidence limits: the research we build on is promising but our approach is not yet validated with real crew data.
  • Next steps: test with public datasets or analog-mission data, and validate with behavioral-health experts.
